title: Acute mesenteric ischaemia
subtitle: Suspect early, CT angiography, revascularise before you resect

sources.title: Management of the Diseases of Mesenteric Arteries and Veins: Clinical Practice Guidelines of the ESVS
Acute mesenteric ischemia: updated guidelines of the World Society of Emergency Surgery

red_flags.text: Severe abdominal pain out of proportion to the examination, especially with AF, recent myocardial infarction or known vascular disease.
Gut emptying (vomiting or diarrhoea) at the onset of pain, in an older patient with a cardiac source. The classic embolic triad.
Post-prandial pain and weight loss before the acute event: acute-on-chronic thrombosis of a mesenteric stenosis.
A critically ill patient on vasopressors, dialysis or after cardiac surgery with new distension, feed intolerance or rising lactate: non-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia.
Peritonitis, blood per rectum or rising lactate: transmural infarction is established and the window for bowel salvage is closing.

do_now.text: CT angiography immediately when acute mesenteric ischaemia is suspected. Do not delay it because of renal function: the risk of missing the diagnosis outweighs the risk to the kidney.
Start intravenous unfractionated heparin once the diagnosis is suspected, unless contraindicated.
Call the vascular and general surgical teams together. This is a two-team operation.
Fluid resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics per local protocol, nasogastric decompression and analgesia.

assess.text: Early on the abdomen may be soft and minimally tender. Signs of peritonitis mean the bowel is already infarcting.
Look for the source: AF, recent infarct, valve disease, previous emboli to the limbs, and a history of mesenteric angina.
Ask about thrombophilia, cancer, oral contraception, portal hypertension and previous venous thrombosis for mesenteric venous thrombosis.
Score organ dysfunction in the critically ill patient; it guides the extent of operation.

investigate.text: Biphasic CT angiography, arterial and portal venous phases, is the diagnostic test of choice for arterial and venous causes.
A normal D-dimer makes acute mesenteric ischaemia unlikely; a raised one is not specific.
Lactate is a late marker. A normal lactate does not exclude ischaemia and must never delay imaging.
FBC, U&E, LFT, amylase, coagulation, gas and group and save. ECG for AF.

resuscitate.text: Correct hypovolaemia and acidosis, and minimise vasoconstrictors where possible because they worsen splanchnic flow.
Non-occlusive ischaemia: treat the low-flow state, and consider intra-arterial vasodilator infusion through the angiography catheter.
Mesenteric venous thrombosis without peritonitis: anticoagulation is the primary treatment.

definitive.text: Peritonitis or suspected infarction: emergency laparotomy. Revascularise the superior mesenteric artery before resecting bowel, because bowel that looks dead may recover once flow returns.
Embolic occlusion: open superior mesenteric embolectomy or endovascular aspiration. Thrombotic occlusion: endovascular stenting, open retrograde stenting or bypass.
Endovascular revascularisation first is reasonable in a patient without peritonitis in a centre that offers it, with laparoscopy or laparotomy to assess the bowel after.
Resect only clearly non-viable bowel, leave the bowel in discontinuity and plan a second-look laparotomy at 24 to 48 hours.

escalate.text: Consultant vascular and general surgeons together for the decision to operate and the plan for revascularisation.
Interventional radiology for endovascular options; transfer to a centre with a hybrid theatre where possible and safe.
Critical care for every operated patient. Discuss futility early when the whole small bowel is infarcted.
Long-term follow-up for anticoagulation, the embolic source and intestinal failure if extensive resection was needed.

notes: The diagnosis is made by suspecting it. Pain out of proportion in an old patient with AF is mesenteric until CT says otherwise.
Flow first, then judge the gut. The colour after revascularisation is the colour that counts.
Do not anastomose ischaemic bowel. Discontinuity and a planned second look are the safe defaults.
